slides: Welcome back. Now similarity in shapes that aren't regular.

slides.say: In regular shapes, the similarity was easy to see. Here it's harder. Not to see that the shapes are similar, but to know what matches what.

slides: This lesson is long and very important, so I'll take it in parts. Let's start with triangles.

slides.say: Similar triangles are triangles whose angles are all equal. And it's enough that two angles are equal.

slides: Why? The three angles of a triangle always add up to a hundred eighty. So if two angles are equal, the third one must be equal too.

slides.say: Here are two triangles. Both have a right angle, and both have an angle of thirty degrees.
So the third angle is a hundred eighty minus ninety minus thirty, sixty, in both of them. They're similar.
But a triangle with ninety and forty degrees isn't similar to them. Its third angle is fifty, not sixty.
Here are two more similar triangles. Both have a right angle.
at: Here are two more similar triangles

slides.say: The other angles are the same in both too. Let's call them alpha and beta.
at: Let's call them alpha and beta

slides.say: In a regular polygon, there's no question of matching. Every side is the same. But in this triangle, the sides are different. There's a short leg, a long leg, and a hypotenuse.

slides: So how do we know which side matches which? Here's the rule. In similar triangles, the matching sides are the sides opposite the equal angles.

slides.say: Twelve is opposite alpha in the small triangle. Opposite alpha in the big one is eighteen. So twelve goes with eighteen.
Sixteen is opposite beta. Opposite beta in the big one is twenty-four. So sixteen goes with twenty-four.
And the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle in both. So twenty goes with thirty.
at: the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle

slides.say: Now I strongly recommend something, and I'm telling you this from years of experience.

slides: Students used to work with ratios and divisions, the way they learned in school. And they got tangled.

slides.say: So make a little table. One column for the small triangle, and one column for the big triangle.
In each row we write one pair of matching sides. Twelve and eighteen, opposite alpha.
Sixteen and twenty-four, opposite beta.
And twenty and thirty, the two hypotenuses.
Look at each row. Eighteen is twelve plus half of twelve. So every row is times one and a half. The table shows us exactly what matches what.
at: So every row is times one and a half

slides.say: The table also finds a missing side. Say we didn't know the twenty-four. We know twelve goes with eighteen, and sixteen goes with a question mark.
at: sixteen goes with a question mark

slides.say: Like in word problems, we use the triangle value. We multiply along the diagonal, and divide by what's left.
The diagonal is sixteen and eighteen, and what's left is twelve. So it's sixteen times eighteen, divided by twelve.
Let's make the numbers smaller first. Eighteen and twelve both divide by six. Eighteen becomes three, and twelve becomes two.
at: Eighteen and twelve both divide by six

slides.say: So it's sixteen times three, divided by two. Sixteen times three is forty-eight, and half of forty-eight is twenty-four. That's our missing side.
Here it was easy, because the triangles stood the same way. But even if we turn a triangle, we can still find the matching sides.
at: even if we turn a triangle

slides.say: Here the big triangle is upside down. We don't look at left or right. We look at the angles.
Eighteen is still opposite alpha, and twenty-four is still opposite beta. So the pairs haven't changed.
And here's something useful. The ratio between two sides of the same triangle is also equal in both triangles.
Twelve over sixteen is three quarters. Eighteen over twenty-four is also three quarters.
at: Twelve over sixteen is three quarters

slides.say: Another pair. Sixteen over twenty is four fifths, and twenty-four over thirty is four fifths too.
at: Sixteen over twenty is four fifths

slides.say: Until now we wrote ratios with a colon, like four to five. A fraction is exactly the same thing. We write it as a fraction, because fractions are easy to reduce. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
